title: iPhone 16e schematics made public by the FCC despite Apple’s confidentiality request
snippet: A 163-page PDF of the iPhone 16e electrical schematics was briefly made public by the FCC, despite Apple’s express request to keep them confidential. Here’s what they showed. more…
fullText:
A 163-page PDF of the iPhone 16e electrical schematics was briefly made public by the FCC, despite Apple’s express request to keep them confidential. Here’s what they showed.

What happened?

Over the weekend, secret electric schematics for the iPhone 16e models A3212/A3408/A3409/A3410 were briefly made public in the FCC’s equipment authorization database, and were mirrored by fccid.io before being pulled.

The filing included a separate letter in which Apple requested confidentiality for the schematics and block diagrams, and the documents remained online long enough to be noticed and downloaded.

The publishing of these documents was likely the result of a mistake by a certification body or lab during the filing process. The metadata showed that short-term confidentiality and permanent confidentiality were marked as “no,” contrary to Apple’s explicit request, which likely caused them to be auto-published by FCCID.io.

How serious is this leak?

That depends. For end users of the iPhone 16e, it’s not that serious. But the electrical schematics detail board-level components, antenna locations, connectors, block diagrams, test pads, and other parts of the logic board, which is information that could be highly relevant to hardware researchers and even independent repair shops.

The schematics can also offer insight into how Apple routes signals between major chips, how test/debug pads are laid out, and what hidden traces exist inside the “sandwich” logic board. In a nutshell, this makes fault tracing and board repair easier, and it could help security researchers identify potentially new hardware attack surfaces.

So far, Apple and the FCC haven’t commented on the leak.

fullText:
MagSafe batteries are one of my favorite types of accessories because they let you keep your iPhone charged without needing to find a wall adapter (verbal meme: zombies, but it’s tech people looking for a wall plug) The new CP12 MagSafe Power Bank has a 10,000mAh battery, offers 20W wired charging, 7.5W MagSafe charging, and even includes a built in cable for when you want to charge a bit faster. It is not the slimmest battery, but it gives you plenty of flexibility for travel, commuting, or just making sure your iPhone lasts all day.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Design and build quality

The CP12 is not a tiny MagSafe battery at all, but it feels very well built. The magnetic attachment is strong enough to stay in place once it snaps onto your iPhone. The manufacturer says it is rated to hold up to 1000g, which is more than five times the weight of an iPhone 16. It feels secure enough to use while walking around or scrolling on the couch. The braided cable is a nice touch as well, and it feels more durable than a standard cable.

The CP12 does add some bulk, especially compared to smaller 5,000mAh MagSafe batteries, but the tradeoff is that you get a lot more capacity. If you want one battery pack to get you through travel days or long commutes, this size makes sense. If you need something for the afternoon, there are different options. There is a world where you end up with multiple types and sizes of MagSafe batteries.

Charging performance

The CP12 supports 7.5W MagSafe charging for MagSafe and Qi wireless devices. It works well for keeping your iPhone topped up throughout the day, but it’s not the fastest out there. One nice benefit of the slower speed is that it helps manage heat, so the phone should not trigger the overheated alert as much. Especially during the summer, I would see that alert a lot if I was outside all day.

The built-in cable gives you up to 20W, which makes a noticeable difference when you want to quickly add battery before heading out the door. It also supports 20W input charging, so the battery itself can recharge quickly when plugged in. Again, it’s not what I want to do daily, but I love having the option. If I am low on battery and outside in the heat, I might opt to use the wired option for speed, but if I am on an airplane, I’ll be fine with the MagSafe charging option. The cable is also nice for charging a Nintendo Switch, AirPods Pro, or other devices.

The only downside to the CUKTECH CP12 is size. It is thicker than smaller, lower-capacity MagSafe packs, and you will feel it in your pocket. But that is the tradeoff for the extra battery life and features. For travel and commuting, I think the size is worth it.

Wrap up on the CP12

The CP12 MagSafe Power Bank delivers a lot of functionality in one accessory. Between the strong magnetic hold, 10,000mAh capacity, 20W wired charging, and the built in cable, it covers almost every use case you would want from a portable charger. title: New iPhone game RidePods uses clever AirPods trick for steering
snippet: AirPods are always getting better, and iOS 26 recently added a bunch of new features. But a new game on the App Store, RidePods, takes AirPods in a unique and clever new direction as game controllers. more…
fullText:
AirPods are always getting better, and iOS 26 recently added a bunch of new features. But a new game on the App Store, RidePods, takes AirPods in a unique and clever new direction as game controllers.

RidePods game uses motion tracking in AirPods for hands-free steering

As first highlighted by The Verge, the new game RidePods (App Store link) enables you to use AirPods as a sort of game controller.

Except you won’t be reaching up to touch your AirPods at all—that wouldn’t exactly be the most comfortable game mechanic.

Instead, RidePods is a racing game that lets you steer completely hands-free thanks to AirPods.

The game utilizes AirPods’ head tracking features that power features like spatial audio, but puts them to use for gaming.

How it works is pretty simple: when playing RidePods, your motorcycle steers left and right based on the movements of your head while wearing AirPods.

I found the mechanic a fun, intuitive twist on iPhone gaming. Would I want to play anything for hours using head tracking with AirPods? No, but it still makes for a unique experience.

RidePods supports AirPods models that offer head tracking features. That includes:

AirPods Pro, AirPods Pro 2, and AirPods Pro 3

AirPods 3 and AirPods 4

AirPods Max

You can download RidePods for free on the App Store.

Are you interested in seeing more games add support for AirPods head tracking like RidePods? Let us know in the comments.
